results.name: yes_trial_index_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on trial_index (per 100 trials); observed more negative than null means people drift toward saying no over the session, which the stimulus-only model does not produce.
results.code:
# name: yes_trial_index_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on trial_index (per 100 trials); observed more negative than null means people drift toward saying no over the session, which the stimulus-only model does not produce.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return E, t, r

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy() / 100.0
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    xc = x - x.mean()
    return float((xc * (r - r.mean())).sum() / max((xc ** 2).sum(), 1e-9))

results.name: parity_violation_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all even or all odd, yes rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed above null means people commit to parity-consistent rules less than the model (model too all-or-none), below means more.
results.code:
# name: parity_violation_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all even or all odd, yes rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed above null means people commit to parity-consistent rules less than the model (model too all-or-none), below means more.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return E, t, r

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r = _ex(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, E % 2)
    s = np.nansum(par, 1)
    alleven = s == 0; allodd = s == n
    m = (n >= 2) & ((alleven & (t % 2 == 1)) | (allodd & (t % 2 == 0)))
    return _rate(r, m)

results.name: single_example_nonexample_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets after a single-example set; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example (too strong size principle/commitment), below means too broadly.
results.code:
# name: single_example_nonexample_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets after a single-example set; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example (too strong size principle/commitment), below means too broadly.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return E, t, r

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r = _ex(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    m = (n == 1) & ~(E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return _rate(r, m)

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 away from every example; observed above null means people give more distant, rule-unrelated yeses (heavier tails/guessing) than the model's lapse allows.

results.name: within_set_response_variance
results.description: Mean over number sets (with 10+ trials) of the per-set yes-rate variance p(1-p); observed above null means human responses to a set are more mixed across targets than the model's predictions (less all-or-none), below means more polarized.

results.name: shared_tens_digit_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets sharing the tens digit (same decade, e.g. 42 vs 47) with some example but not its last digit; observed above null means people use decade/leading-digit similarity the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: shared_tens_digit_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets sharing the tens digit (same decade, e.g. 42 vs 47) with some example but not its last digit; observed above null means people use decade/leading-digit similarity the model lacks.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return E, t, r

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r = _ex(df)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    tens = (np.floor(E / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    last = ((E % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None]).any(1)
    m = tens & ~last & ~isex & (t < 100)
    return _rate(r, m)

results.name: near_outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets lying just outside the examples' range (1-5 below the minimum or above the maximum); observed above null means people extend intervals past the examples more than the model's similarity/interval account predicts.
results.code:
# name: near_outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets lying just outside the examples' range (1-5 below the minimum or above the maximum); observed above null means people extend intervals past the examples more than the model's similarity/interval account predicts.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return E, t, r

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r = _ex(df)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, 1); hi = np.nanmax(E, 1)
    d = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0))
    m = (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)
    return _rate(r, m)
